explanation: Kwaa Mensah was a Ghanaian highlife musician and the leader of the Fanti Trio, one of the pioneering guitar-band highlife groups of the mid-20th century. He popularised the guitar-band style of highlife across Ghana and West Africa. The Accra Orchestra (B) was a different ensemble. Ghana Combo (C) and Jazz Kings (D) are not associated with Kwaa Mensah. His work with the Fanti Trio established him as a foundational figure in West African popular music.

Pizzicato is an Italian musical term meaning 'plucked.' It is a performance technique for string instruments where the player plucks the strings with the fingers instead of using the bow. Options A (pointed), C (pushed), and D (painted) have no meaning in music terminology. Pizzicato produces a short, dry, percussive tone distinct from the sustained sound of bowing (arco), and is widely used in orchestral and chamber music.

Arnold Schoenberg was the composer who developed and championed atonality — music that abandons traditional key centres and tonal hierarchy. He later formalised this into the twelve-tone (serialism) technique. Stravinsky (A) used polytonality and neo-classicism but not full atonality. Schubert (C) was a Romantic composer working firmly within tonal harmony. Smetana (D) was a Czech nationalist composer who also remained tonal. Schoenberg's atonal works such as Pierrot Lunaire are landmark compositions.

Vivace is an Italian tempo marking meaning 'fast and lively' — one of the faster tempos in classical music, faster than allegro but slightly below presto. Slow (A) would be described by terms like adagio or lento. Sustained (B) is legato — a style of playing, not a tempo. Slow and steady (C) approximates andante or moderato. Vivace's root word 'vivace' comes from Latin 'vivax' meaning lively or full of life.

The Romantic period in Western classical music is generally dated from approximately 1780–1898, beginning with the late works of Haydn and Mozart transitioning into Beethoven, and ending with the late Romantics like Brahms, Tchaikovsky, and early Wagner. Option A (1820–1890) starts too late and ends too early. Option B (1820–1895) also starts too late. Option D (1820–1875) excludes major late-Romantic composers. The JAMB curriculum identifies option C (1780–1898) as the correct range.

In D major, the scale degrees are: D (tonic), E (supertonic), F# (mediant), G (subdominant), A (dominant), B (submediant), C# (leading tone). Note B is the 6th degree, which is the submediant. Option B (mediant) is F#; option C (dominant) is A; option D (subdominant) is G. Counting up from D: D=1, E=2, F#=3, G=4, A=5, B=6 — confirming B is the submediant.

The gulum (also spelled goge in some traditions) is a one-stringed bowed lute found in northern Nigeria and West Africa. Because it produces sound through vibrating strings, it is classified as a chordophone — instruments that produce sound via vibrating strings. An idiophone (A) produces sound through the vibration of the instrument body itself (e.g., bells, clappers). An aerophone (C) produces sound via vibrating air (e.g., flutes). A membranophone (D) uses a stretched membrane (e.g., drums).

Ars Antiqua ('ancient art') and Ars Nova ('new art') are both terms describing musical styles of the Medieval period — Ars Antiqua from the 12th–13th century and Ars Nova from the 14th century. Both belong to the Medieval era, before the Renaissance. The Romantic period (A) is 18th–19th century; the Baroque period (B) is 17th–early 18th century; the Classical period (C) is mid-to-late 18th century. All of these postdate both Ars Nova and Ars Antiqua.

Rock The Party is a popular song by D'banj, the Nigerian Afrobeats and R&B artist. D'banj (Dapo Daniel Oyebanjo) had several major hits in the 2000s under the Mo' Hits record label, and Rock The Party was among his popular tracks. Danny Young (A), Big Bamo (B), and Dijnee (C) are other Nigerian artists but are not associated with this particular song. D'banj's distinctive style and collaborations made him one of Nigeria's most recognised artists of that era.

We Are H.A.P.P.Y is a well-known Nigerian song sung in unison with a strong rhythmic pulse, typically performed while marching — making it a marching song. Praising songs (A) are used in worship or celebration with a slower, devotional character. Art songs (C) are composed for solo voice with piano accompaniment in a classical style. Work songs (D) help coordinate manual labour rhythms. The structured, rhythmic, group-movement nature of We Are H.A.P.P.Y classifies it as a marching song.

Lucky Dube was a South African reggae artist who made a significant contribution to the development and popularisation of reggae music across Africa in the 1980s and 1990s. His socially conscious lyrics and authentic reggae style gave the genre deep roots on the African continent. Manu Dibango (A) is associated with Afrobeat/jazz. Awilo Longomba (B) is known for Congolese rumba. Kofi Olomide (C) is a Congolese soukous artist.

The Ekpo masquerade is a powerful ancestral masquerade cult of the Ibibio people of Akwa Ibom and Cross River States in southern Nigeria. It represents the spirits of the dead and plays important roles in community governance, social control, and traditional ceremonies. The Eggon (A) are from Nasarawa State; the Urhobo (B) have their own distinct masquerades; the Agatu (C) are a minority group in Benue State. Ekpo is distinctively Ibibio.

The classical (12-bar) blues is built on a standard 12-bar chord progression in the pattern I-I-I-I / IV-IV-I-I / V-IV-I-I (or V-I), repeated as the structural foundation for improvisation and lyrics. This 12-bar structure is one of the most influential frameworks in all of popular music. 8-bar blues (B) is a variation; 16-bar blues (C) is less common; 32-bar (A) is a standard song form (AABA) used in pop and jazz, not blues.

Mamman Shata (Mamman Shata Katsina) was a legendary Hausa musician from Katsina State best known for his mastery of the kalangu — the hourglass tension drum (talking drum) used in Hausa and Fulani musical traditions. He used the kalangu to deliver social commentary, praise songs, and historical narratives. Duma (A), tandu (B), and goge (C) are also Hausa musical genres or instruments, but Mamman Shata's signature was the kalangu.

The Nigerian National Anthem ('Arise O Compatriots') is structured in two stanzas with the same melodic pattern repeated — making its musical form stanzaic (also called strophic). Each stanza uses the same melody with different words. Responsorial (A) involves alternating between a leader and group. Ternary (C) is an ABA form. The repetition of the same melody for each text stanza is the defining feature of the stanzaic/strophic form.

A standard string quartet consists of 2 violins (violin I and violin II), 1 viola, and 1 cello. This combination, established in the Classical era by Haydn, provides a balanced four-voice texture covering soprano, alto, tenor, and bass registers. Option A replaces the viola with a double bass, giving a heavier bass sound not typical of the string quartet. Option C replaces the cello with a double bass. Option D has only one violin and two violas, which is an unusual non-standard combination.

The Eki-gene is a traditional cultural dance of the Ijaw people of Bayelsa State in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria. It is performed during festivals and celebrations, characterised by rhythmic movements and colourful costumes. Delta State (B), Rivers State (C), and Edo State (D) have their own distinct dances. The Eki-gene belongs specifically to the Ijaw cultural heritage of Bayelsa.

Aerophones are instruments that produce sound through vibrating columns of air. Kaho (a flute-type instrument), popolo, and ekutu are all wind instruments found in Nigerian musical traditions and therefore classified as aerophones. Option A (molo, komo, kukuma) includes string instruments (chordophones). Option B (bata, bembe, shantu) are drums (membranophones). Option D (ogene, oyo, ekpili) are percussion/metal idiophones. Wind-based instruments = aerophones.

Missa Brevis ('Short Mass') — the most well-known setting — was composed by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, the Italian Renaissance composer whose polyphonic choral style became the model for Catholic sacred music. G.F. Handel (B) wrote large oratorios like the Messiah. Monteverdi (C) composed early opera and madrigals. J.S. Bach (D) also wrote a Missa Brevis, but Palestrina's is the definitive JAMB textbook reference for this title.

Umoja (meaning 'unity' in Swahili) is a South African entertainment company and theatrical dance group known for its energetic performances celebrating African culture. The group gained international fame for their touring productions. Ivory Coast (B), Togo (C), and Nigeria (D) have their own dance traditions and groups, but Umoja is specifically South African. Its Swahili name reflects the pan-African identity embraced by post-apartheid South Africa.

Can We Chill? is a popular R&B song recorded by Ne-Yo (Shaffer Chimere Smith), released in 2005 on his debut. Ne-Yo is known for his smooth vocal style and R&B songwriting. Usher (A) has hits like Yeah! and Confessions but not this song. Dr. Dre (B) is primarily a hip-hop producer and rapper. 50 Cents (D) is a hip-hop artist. Ne-Yo's distinctive falsetto and the song's romantic theme make it one of his signature early tracks.

Swing Low, Sweet Chariot is one of the most well-known Negro spirituals — religious folk songs created by enslaved African Americans in the 18th and 19th centuries. It draws on biblical imagery (the chariot of Elijah) to express hope for freedom and salvation. Cha-cha-cha (A) is a Cuban dance rhythm. Bolero (B) is a slow Spanish/Latin dance. Tango (C) is an Argentine couple dance. Negro spirituals are defined by their African American enslaved origin and spiritual/religious text.

I Call It Love is a song by Lionel Richie, the American R&B and pop singer-songwriter known for classics like Hello, All Night Long, and Say You Say Me. Kelvin Lyttle (B) is known for Turn Me On, not this song. Stevie Wonder (C) and Isaac Hayes (D) are also legendary artists but did not record this particular song. Lionel Richie released I Call It Love from his 2006 album Coming Home.

The Allemande is a Baroque dance of German origin that is typically written in moderate 4/4 time (common time). It was a standard movement in the Baroque dance suite, usually the first movement, followed by the Courante, Sarabande, and Gigue. Option A (3/4) is the Minuet or Sarabande. Option C (3/2) is the Courante. Option D (6/4) is a compound duple metre not typical of the Allemande. The moderate 4/4 flow of the Allemande is its defining rhythmic characteristic.

Martellato is an Italian musical term from 'martello' (hammer), meaning to strike or play with a firm, hammered, accented stroke. On string instruments, it is a bowing technique producing short, forceful detached strokes. On piano, it means striking the keys with a hammering, accented touch. Options A (pinched), C (blasted), and D (punched) are not recognised musical terms. Hammered (B) is the direct translation and correct meaning.

An incantation is a set of special words, chants, or formulas believed to have magical or supernatural effects when spoken or sung. Incantations feature prominently in African traditional religion, traditional medicine, and oral literature. Heaving (A) refers to a breathing or lifting action. Whistling (B) is a simple sound technique. Recitative (C) is a vocal style in opera used to advance the narrative. Only incantation specifically refers to words with supposed magical power.

Adara is a popular song by Nigerian artist Sasha (Adetoun Onajobi), a female R&B and Afropop singer who gained fame in the mid-2000s. Weird MC (A) is known for Ijoya. Olu Maintain (B) is known for Nawti. Alex (D) is not associated with this song. Sasha's Adara was a widely played track that helped establish her as a notable female voice in Nigerian music during that era.

The Folk Symphony is a major orchestral work by Fela Sowande (1905–1987), one of Nigeria's greatest classical composers. In this composition, Sowande blended Nigerian folk melodies with Western orchestral forms, making it a landmark of Nigerian art music and nationalistic composition. Akin Euba (A) is a contemporary Nigerian composer of a different generation. Bode Omojola (C) is a musicologist. Ayo Bankole (D) was a composer but the Folk Symphony is specifically Sowande's.

Griots (also called Jeli) of Senegambia are hereditary wandering musicians, storytellers, historians, and praise-singers who travel between communities and royal courts, performing at ceremonies, weddings, and important events. They are not tied to a single palace (A), village (D), or cult (C). Their role as itinerant keepers and performers of oral tradition across multiple communities defines them as wandering musicians in the West African social system.

A standard string quartet consists of four instruments: 2 violins (first violin and second violin), 1 viola, and 1 cello (B). This combination provides the full range from soprano (first violin) through alto (second violin and viola) to bass (cello). Option A replaces the viola with a double bass — too low and no viola. Option C uses viola and double bass — loses the balanced middle register. Option D uses only one violin and two violas — nonstandard combination.

The Eki-gene is a traditional cultural dance originating from Bayelsa State (A) in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria. It is performed among the Ijaw/Izon people of Bayelsa during festivals, ceremonies, and celebrations. It should not be confused with Delta State (B), Rivers State (C), or Edo State (D) dances, though these states share cultural proximity in the Niger Delta.

Aerophones are instruments that produce sound primarily through vibrating air. Kaho, popolo, and ekutu (C) are wind instruments (aerophones) from Nigerian traditional music. Molo, komo, and kukuma (A) are chordophones (stringed instruments). Bata, bembe, and shantu (B) are membranophones (drum-type instruments). Ogene, oyo, and ekpili (D) are idiophones (instruments that produce sound by their own vibration). Only option C lists wind/aerophone instruments.

Missa Brevis (meaning 'Short Mass') has been composed by many composers, but in the WAEC music curriculum context, the Missa Brevis most associated with early polyphony is attributed to Giovanni Palestrina (A) (c.1525–1594), the Italian Renaissance composer known for sacred polyphonic music. G.F. Handel (B) composed oratorios. Monteverdi (C) composed madrigals and early opera. J.S. Bach (D) composed the Missa Brevis in G, but Palestrina's is most referenced in this context.

Umoja (meaning 'unity' in Swahili) is a South African (A) theatrical dance production and traditional dance group known for celebrating Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Tsonga, and other South African cultures through dance, music, and acrobatics. It has been performed internationally. It is not from Ivory Coast (B), Togo (C), or Nigeria (D).

'Can We Chill?' is a popular R&B song recorded by Ne-Yo (C) (Shaffer Chimere Smith), the American singer and songwriter. It was released as one of his notable tracks. Usher (A) and Dr. Dre (B) have not recorded this specific song. 50 Cent (D) is primarily a rapper known for different tracks. Ne-Yo composed this song.

An augmented triad sounds bright and tense. A minor triad (B) has a minor third + perfect fifth. A diminished triad (C) has a minor third + diminished fifth. A major triad (D) has a major third + perfect fifth.

This question references a triad shown in a score image that is not available. Based on the answer (C — first inversion), the triad shown has its third in the bass (lowest position). In first inversion, the third of the chord is the lowest note (e.g., E-G-C in C major chord). Root position (D) has the root in the bass. Second inversion (B) has the fifth in the bass. Third inversion (A) applies only to seventh chords. The first inversion places the third at the bottom.

A semibreve (whole note) = 32 demisemiquavers; a minim (half note) = 16 demisemiquavers; a crotchet (quarter note) = 8 demisemiquavers. The note shown is most likely a minim (half note), which equals 16 demisemiquavers.

Transposing 3½ tones (7 semitones = a perfect 5th) upward from any starting key raises the pitch by a perfect fifth. Without the score image showing the original key, the answer relies on the given answer of C (G major). If the original passage is in C major, transposing up a perfect 5th gives G major. If the original is in another key, the same interval upward yields a different key. The answer is G major (C).

D major is identified by its key signature (two sharps) or the final note/tonic of the melody being D. The key has a bright, assertive character commonly used in orchestral and choral music.

'I Call It Love' is a well-known hit song by Lionel Richie (A), the legendary American singer and songwriter. It was a popular adult contemporary ballad. Kelvin Lyttle (B) is known for 'Turn Me On'. Stevie Wonder (C) has different hit songs. Isaac Hayes (D) is known for the 'Shaft' theme and soul music. Lionel Richie is specifically associated with 'I Call It Love'.
